# Picking up from last lecture: bootstrap for regression inference




# Review: Multiple Linear Regression

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Example: Reed Theses 

How does **Page Count** ($y$) vary by **Year** ($x_1$) and **Division** ($x_2$)?


```{r out.width="95%",fig.asp=.45}
ggplot(theses, aes(x = year, y = n_pages, color = division))+
  geom_point(alpha = .5)+labs(x="Year",y="Number of Pages",color="Division")+
  geom_parallel_slopes(method = "lm", se = F)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Example: Reed Theses 

How does **Page Count** ($y$) vary by **Year** ($x_1$) and **Division** ($x_2$)?

```{r echo=T}
mod_YearDivision <- lm(n_pages ~ year + division, data = theses)
get_regression_table(mod_YearDivision)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Review: Multiple Regression Model

```{r echo=T}
mod_YearDivision <- lm(n_pages ~ year + division, data = theses)
get_regression_table(mod_YearDivision)
```

<br>

We assume in the **[population]{.underline}**, the response $y$ is a linear function of the explanatory variables $x_1,\dots,x_k$:

$$
y  = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots + \beta_k x_k + \epsilon
$$


But we estimate the model from the **[sample]{.underline}** data that we actually have:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{y}  &= \widehat{\beta_0} + \widehat{\beta_1}  x_1 + \widehat{\beta_2}  x_2 + \dots + \widehat{\beta_k}  x_k\\
&= 626 -0.284 \cdot \text{Year} + 33.2 \cdot \text{HSS} + 22.7 \cdot \text{LL} - 4.99 \cdot \text{MNS} + 21.1 \cdot \text{PRPL}
\end{aligned}
$$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Review: Interpretation

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{y}  &= 626 -0.284 \cdot \text{Year} + 33.2 \cdot \text{HSS} + 22.7 \cdot \text{LL} - 4.99 \cdot \text{MNS} + 21.1 \cdot \text{PRPL}
\end{aligned}
$$

<br>

- [Intercept:]{.underline} The **[expected/predicted]** number of pages (y) for a thesis in **year 0** and for the **baseline division** (Arts) is 626 pages, **on average**


- [Quantitative Slope:]{.underline} For a **one-year increase in time**, we **[expect/predict]** a 0.284 page decrease in thesis length **on average**, holding **division constant**.



- [Categorical Slope:]{.underline} Comparing a thesis in the **HSS division to the baseline division (Arts)**, we **[expect/predict]** a 33.2 page increase in thesis length, **on average**, holding **year constant**.


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Review: Conditions

We want linear regression models to satisfy 4 conditions:



1. **Linearity:** The relationship between explanatory and response variables must be approximately linear
    - Check using scatterplot/residual plot
    



2. **Independence:** The observations should be independent of one another.
    - Assess using context!




3. **Normality:** The distribution of residuals should be normally distributed
    - Histogram of residuals
    - Q-Q plot of residuals
    



4. **Equal Variability:** Variance of residuals should be roughly constant across data set. 
    - Check using scatterplot/residual plot.
    

------------------------------------------------------------------------    

## Code for Checking Conditions

::::: columns

::: column

**Residual plot**: Residuals vs fitted values

```{r echo=T, fig.height = 6}
mod_YearDivision %>% 
  get_regression_points() %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n_pages_hat, y = residual))+
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = F)
```

:::

::: column

**Residuals histogram and Q-Q Plot**

```{r echo=T, fig.height = 2.5}
mod_YearDivision %>% 
  get_regression_points() %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = residual)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, color = "white")
```


```{r echo=T, fig.height = 2.5}
mod_YearDivision %>% 
  get_regression_points() %>%
  ggplot(aes(sample = residual)) +
  geom_qq() + 
  geom_qq_line()
```

:::

:::::


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Inference Procedures

- We can proceed with coefficient-level inference for Multiple Linear Regression exactly the same way we did for Simple Linear Regression! 

::::: columns

::: {.column width=45%}

- [If ALL of the LINE conditions are satisfied]{.underline}
    - Use theory-based inference!
    - Confidence intervals and coefficient-level hypothesis tests given by `get_regression_table()` function

:::

::: {.column width=55%}

- [If at least Linearity and Independence are satisfied]{.underline}
    - Resampling-based inference
    - Use resampling methods to create confidence intervals and coefficient-level hypothesis tests
    - More practice on next week's lab
    
:::

:::::
  
- [ALWAYS]{.underline}
    - Check adjusted $R^2$ using `get_regression_summaries()` function
    - Consider *statistical* [AND]{.underline} *practical* significance
    - Look at plots (e.g., exploratory plots, regression model plots, plots for assumptions)
  



# Model Selection

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Background: Model Selection

- Often, we have a more generic goal than learning about a specific coefficient:
    - **What's the [best]{.underline} model to predict $y$ using some combination of variables $x_1$, $x_2$,\dots,$x_k$?**

<br>

- A few options:
    - "Smallest" model: Intercept-only model (i.e., no predictors at all!) 
    - "Biggest model: Include all variables and their interactions 
    - Something in between? 
  
<!-- ::: fragment -->

<!-- **Think-Pair-Share:** How might you pick the "best" model? -->

<!-- ::: -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| echo: false -->
<!-- countdown::countdown(3) -->
<!-- ``` -->
  

------------------------------------------------------------------------
  
## Things to Avoid

There is no single correct way to pick a model...but there are "bad" ways

1. **Fitting the biggest model and only keeping variables with "significant" p-values**
    - Variables can be interrelated. We may remove groups of variables which add value to our model!
    - Ideally, we should be able to justify why each variable is included in the model, beyond "the p-value told me to"
  
  
2. **Forward selection and Backward selection**
    - Some statisticians used to advocate for successively adding/removing variables based on highest/lowest p-values.
    - This can be inaccurate, noisy, and messes with our type-I error rate


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## How to Engage in Model Selection

Three recommended tools for model selection:


1. **Context:** Do we have a contextual reason to believe a variable should be included? 
    - Talk to experts; examine data plots; hypothesize 




2. **Parsimony:** Is there a simpler model that's about as good?
    - Examine data plots, see how $R^2$ changes




3. **"Nested F-tests":** Hypothesis test for including groups of variables in our model
    - We'll learn about this today!


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## More Penguins

Let's again predict Bill Length ($y$) with Species ($x_1$) and Body Mass ($x_2$) 

```{r warning=FALSE, fig.height=5}
ggplot(data=penguins,aes(x=body_mass_g,color=species,y=bill_length_mm))+
  geom_point()+theme(legend.position = c(.9,.25))+
  labs(x="Body Mass",y="Bill Length",color="Species")
```

 

- Context: We can see Body Mass and Species are related to Bill Length (and this probably aligns with our hypotheses)

- Should we include interaction terms? (consider parsimony)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Nested F-Tests

The **Nested F-Test** is designed for these situations: 

It compares two "nested" models:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{"Small" Model:} \quad &y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 +\dots+\beta_mx_m\\
\text{"Large" Model:} \quad &y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 +\dots+\beta_mx_m + \beta_{m+1}x_{m+1} + \dots + \beta_px_p
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.fragment}

**Hypotheses**
$$
\begin{aligned}
H_0:& \text{ The small model is sufficient at explaining y}\\
H_a:& \text{ The large model is superior to the small at explaining y}\\
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

- Models **MUST** be "nested"

- Condition: "Large" model *should* satisfy LINE conditions

- We'll learn more about F-tests in the next lecture. For now, let R do the work.

- **Q**: If we get a very small ($< \alpha$) p-value from our F-test, what should we conclude? 


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Nested F-Tests

```{r echo=T}
# Setting up our models
model_small <- lm(bill_length_mm ~ body_mass_g + species, data = penguins)
model_large <- lm(bill_length_mm ~ body_mass_g * species, data = penguins)
```

<br> 

```{r echo=T}
# We'll learn more about what anova() is doing next time!!
# Small model first, large model second
anova(model_small, model_large)
```

<br>

- We have a p-value of 0.20 $\implies$ insufficient evidence to reject the null.
  
- Thus, we should use the "small" model (without interaction effects!)
  

------------------------------------------------------------------------
  
## Word of Caution

Suppose you had fit the small and large models and compared each coefficient's p-value:

```{r}
small <- get_regression_table(model_small) %>% select(term,p_value)
names(small)[2] <- "pvals SMALL model"
res <- get_regression_table(model_large) %>% select(term,p_value) %>%
  left_join(small) %>% select(term,`pvals SMALL model`,p_value)
names(res)[3] <- "pvals LARGE model"
kableExtra::kable(res)
```


::: {.fragment .nonincremental}

**Think-Pair-Share:**

- What variables would you have kept if you only looked at p-values in the "large" model?

- What do you notice? Are you surprised?

- Can you explain this behavior?

<!-- Interaction term changes the interpretation: species coefficients now represent expected/predicted change in bill length for that particular species vs reference level when the body mass is 0 - bigger extrapolation and less data than estimating constant shift between species, holding body mass constant. -->

:::

## Final Note: Model Selection

- There are tons of other tools for model selection:
    - "Goodness-of-Fit" criteria, like AIC and BIC
    - Penalized regression, like the "lasso" and "ridge regression"
    - Cross validation
  
- These are covered in Math 243!
